mainTopic: Careful speech (רב and רבי חייא, הלכות of אבלות, דן and זבולון), then why בדיקת חמץ is at night and the rules for a house rented on the fourteenth
overview: The amud opens with stories about careful speech. רב arrives in ארץ ישראל, and his uncle רבי חייא asks about his family. רב hints with questions that both his parents have died, and from רבי חייא's brief mourning the גמרא learns three הלכות of אבלות. Two short stories then show that a person's habitual speech can reveal his שבט, דן or זבולון. The גמרא returns to בדיקת חמץ and asks why we search at night when חמץ is only forbidden from the sixth hour. רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that people are home at night and a candle searches well, and אביי rules that a scholar should not start learning that night. The גמרא then asks who must check a house rented on the fourteenth, and a ברייתא answers that it depends on when the keys were handed over. Finally it asks whether a rented house is presumed checked, and רב נחמן בר יצחק begins answering from the rule that everyone is believed about removing חמץ. The reason for that trust is given on the next amud.

steps.title: Background: רב's unusual family tie to רבי חייא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רב was both the nephew of רבי חייא through his brother and the nephew of רבי חייא through his sister.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב was the son of רבי חייא's brother, and also the son of רבי חייא's sister.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a story. It first gives background on how רב and רבי חייא were related.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's father אייבו and his mother אימא were half-siblings of רבי חייא from different parents, and they married each other. So רבי חייא is רב's uncle on both sides. This explains why the next question about אייבו and אימא is so personal: they are רבי חייא's own brother and sister.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not forbidden. אייבו and אימא were half-siblings of רבי חייא through different parents, so they were step-siblings to each other, not blood relatives.

phrases.english: Rav was the son of Rabbi Chiya's brother
phrases.notes: רב's father was אייבו, רבי חייא's half-brother.

phrases.english: and the son of his sister.
phrases.notes: רב's mother was אימא, רבי חייא's half-sister.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב, בַּר אֲחוּהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא וּבַר אֲחָתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story that continues the earlier theme of refined and careful speech.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב was רבי חייא's nephew through both his father and his mother.

steps.title: רבי חייא asks whether his brother is alive
steps.stepSummary: When רב arrives in ארץ ישראל, רבי חייא asks him whether his father אייבו is still alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב went up to ארץ ישראל, רבי חייא asked him: Is אייבו alive?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא asks a simple family question. This sets up רב's careful answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חייא wants to know if his brother אייבו is alive. In fact, he had died. That puts רב in an awkward spot: how do you give bad news without saying it bluntly?

keyTerms.meaning: when he went up there, meaning to ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: When he went up there,
phrases.notes: 'There' means ארץ ישראל. רב came from בבל.

phrases.english: he (Rabbi Chiya) said to him: Is Ayevu alive?
phrases.notes: רבי חייא asks about רב's father, his own brother.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי סְלֵיק לְהָתָם, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַיְיבוּ קַיָּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the family background to begin the conversation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is רב's father אייבו still alive?

steps.title: רב answers with questions instead of saying 'he died'
steps.stepSummary: רב answers each question with another question, hinting that both of his parents had died without saying so directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Is אימא alive?! רבי חייא then asked: Is אימא alive? רב said: Is אייבו alive?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב avoids saying the painful words 'he died.' He answers with questions, and רבי חייא understands from this that both אייבו and אימא had passed away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When asked about his father, רב responds as if to say, 'Did you think my mother is still alive?' When רבי חייא then asks about the mother, רב responds, 'Did you think my father is still alive?' This way רב passes on the bad news about both parents without ever saying a harsh word, an example of careful speech.

keyTerms.meaning: Imma, the name of רב's mother, also רבי חייא's sister

steps.whyThisMatters: This story fits the larger theme of the סוגיא: a refined person avoids blunt or unpleasant language, especially when giving bad news.
steps.confusionAlert: The second question is רבי חייא asking again, and the last line is רב answering. רב is not actually asking for information. His questions are a gentle way of saying 'no.'

phrases.english: He (Rav) said to him: Is Imma alive?!
phrases.notes: רב answers with a hint: my mother is gone, and my father too.

phrases.english: He (Rabbi Chiya) said to him: Is Imma alive?
phrases.notes: רבי חייא now asks directly about his sister.

phrases.english: He (Rav) said to him: Is Ayevu alive?!
phrases.notes: Again a hint: neither parent is alive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי חייא's question in an indirect way.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both אייבו and אימא have died. רב conveys this through questions instead of stating it outright.

steps.title: רבי חייא mourns, then goes to the bathhouse
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא tells his attendant to take off his shoes, a mourning practice, and to carry his clothes to the bathhouse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא said to his attendant: Take off my shoes, and carry my things after me to the bathhouse.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא reacts to the news by beginning to mourn, then soon goes to bathe. The גמרא will learn הלכות from this in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking off shoes is a sign of אבלות. Going to the bathhouse is normally forbidden for an אבל. Doing both, one right after the other, shows that his mourning lasted only a short time.

phrases.english: He (Rabbi Chiya) said to his attendant:
Take off my shoes for me
and carry my things after me to the bathhouse.
phrases.notes: After a short time, the mourning is over and he may bathe.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְשַׁמָּעֵיהּ: חֲלוֹץ לִי מִנְעָלַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רבי חייא's reaction to the news he understood from רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי חייא removed his shoes as an אבל, and right afterward went to the bathhouse.

steps.title: Three laws of mourning learned from רבי חייא's actions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns three הלכות: an אבל may not wear shoes, שמועה רחוקה is mourned for only one day, and מקצת היום ככולו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn three things from this: (1) an אבל may not wear shoes; (2) news that arrives late, a שמועה רחוקה, is mourned for only one day; (3) part of the day counts like the whole day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws three practical הלכות of אבלות from what רבי חייא did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: (1) He took off his shoes, so an אבל is forbidden to wear shoes. (2) His parents had died long before, more than thirty days, and he mourned only one day, so late news gets only one day of mourning. (3) He went to the bathhouse right after starting, so even a small part of that day counts as the whole day of mourning.

keyTerms.meaning: 'distant news': hearing of a death after thirty days have passed
part of the day counts like the whole day

steps.whatToRemember: Three הלכות of אבלות: an אבל may not wear shoes; שמועה רחוקה requires only one day of mourning; and for mourning, מקצת היום ככולו.
steps.whyThisMatters: These are practical הלכות of אבלות that are applied in actual practice.

phrases.english: Learn from this three things.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: אָבֵל אָסוּר בִּנְעִילַת הַסַּנְדָּל.
phrases.english: Learn from it: a mourner is forbidden to wear shoes.
phrases.notes: Because he took off his shoes.

phrases.english: And learn from it: for distant news (a death heard about after thirty days)
mourning is practiced only one day.
And learn from it: part of the day is like the whole of it.
phrases.notes: He went to bathe soon after beginning to mourn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws legal conclusions from רבי חייא's actions in the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An אבל may not wear shoes; שמועה רחוקה is mourned one day; מקצת היום ככולו for אבלות.

steps.title: A man's favorite phrase shows he is from שבט דן
steps.stepSummary: A man always said 'judge my case,' and the חכמים concluded he came from שבט דן, whose name means judging.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man used to say: 'Judge my case.' They said: Learn from this that he comes from דן, as it is written: 'דן will judge his people like one of the tribes of ישראל.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new short story showing that the way a person talks can reveal his family roots.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man's habit of speaking about judging, 'דונו דיני,' matched the nature of שבט דן, whose name comes from the word for judging. The פסוק in יעקב's blessing links דן to judging, so his speech pointed to his ancestry.

keyTerms.meaning: he comes from the tribe of דן

phrases.english: A certain man used to say: Judge my case.
phrases.notes: He said this often, whenever he had a dispute.

phrases.english: They said: Learn from this that he comes from Dan,
as it is written: "Dan will judge his people
like one of the tribes of Israel."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story on the theme of speech: a person's habitual words reveal his background.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who always spoke of judging was identified as coming from שבט דן.

steps.title: A man who praised the seashore turns out to be from זבולון
steps.stepSummary: A man always praised the plants by the sea. They checked his lineage and found he came from שבט זבולון, which lives by the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man would walk around saying: 'The bushes by the sea are cypresses.' They checked and found that he came from זבולון, as it is written: 'זבולון will dwell by the seashore.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second short story with the same lesson: a person's speech reflects his roots.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This man loved everything near the sea and praised even its plain bushes as fine cypresses. When they checked his family, he really was from זבולון, the שבט that יעקב blessed to live by the sea. Unlike the first story, here they actually investigated and confirmed the guess.

keyTerms.meaning: the bushes are cypresses, meaning beautiful trees
they checked and found him to be

steps.whatToRemember: The way a person habitually speaks can reveal his inner nature and even his family roots, as seen with דן and זבולון.

phrases.english: A certain man would walk around and say:
The bushes on the seashore are cypresses.
phrases.notes: Things by the sea are more beautiful than elsewhere.

phrases.english: They checked and found that he came from Zevulun,
as it is written: "Zevulun shall dwell by the seashore."

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּהֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל וְאָמַר: אַכֵּיף יַמָּא אָסֵיסְנִי בִּירָאתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to the one about דן, reinforcing the same lesson.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who always praised the seashore was found to come from שבט זבולון.

steps.title: Why not search at the sixth hour?
steps.stepSummary: Since everyone agrees that 'אור' means evening, the גמרא asks why we search at night. חמץ only becomes forbidden from the sixth hour of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that we know everyone agrees 'אור' means evening, here is a problem. According to both רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר, חמץ is only forbidden from the sixth hour of the day and on. So why not search at the sixth hour?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's rule of searching on the night of the fourteenth and challenges its timing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The search exists so we can get rid of חמץ before it becomes forbidden. Even though רבי יהודה and רבי מאיר argue about the rabbinic deadline, both agree the Torah ban starts at six hours. So the search could seemingly wait until then, and the night seems too early.

keyTerms.meaning: After all, consider this (opens a logical argument)
Six hours (midday), when the Torah ban on חמץ begins

phrases.english: And now that we have established
that according to everyone, "or" means evening,
after all, both according to Rabbi Yehuda
and according to Rabbi Meir,
chametz is not forbidden
except from six hours and onward,
so let us search at six!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side stories about lineage and returns to the משנה's timing of בדיקת חמץ, building on the conclusion that אור means evening.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that we search on the night of the fourteenth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The deadline is the sixth hour, so a search at night is earlier than needed.

steps.title: Even being eager only explains a morning search
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks a possible answer. If the reason is that eager people do מצוות early, that would only move the search to the morning, not the night before.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that eager people do מצוות early, then let us search in the morning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks an answer someone might give to its question, so the question becomes sharper.
steps.deeperAnalysis: זריזין מקדימין למצות means doing a מצוה at the earliest proper time. That time is the morning of the day of the מצוה, not the night before. So this principle still does not explain a nighttime search.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (brings up a possible answer)

phrases.english: And if you say
the eager are early for מצוות,
then let us search from the morning!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Blocks a possible answer to the question of step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The night timing of בדיקת חמץ
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being eager would move the search to the morning, not the night.

steps.title: The source for doing מצוות early: מילה and אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows where זריזין מקדימין comes from. The whole eighth day is fine for מילה, but eager people do it in the morning, like אברהם who rose early.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written, 'On the eighth day his foreskin shall be circumcised.' And a ברייתא teaches: the whole day is fine for מילה, but the eager do מצוות early, as it says, 'And אברהם rose early in the morning.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings proof for the principle it just used. The proof shows that this principle means 'morning of the day,' not 'the night before.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'day,' so מילה can be done all day. Doing it in the morning is just extra eagerness, learned from אברהם at the עקדה. This proves that being early means early in the day, which makes the question on the nighttime search stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it is written:
"And on the eighth day
the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised,"
and it was taught:
the entire day is fit for circumcision,
but the eager are early for מצוות,
as it is said:
"And Abraham rose early in the morning."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the principle used in step 9.
steps.raayaObject: The principle זריזין מקדימין למצות, and that it means the morning
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק about מילה on the eighth day, a ברייתא, and the פסוק 'וישכם אברהם בבקר'
steps.confusionAlert: Steps 9 and 10 are not the גמרא's answer. They make the question harder, because they show that eagerness only leads to a morning search.

steps.title: Night is when people are home and a candle works best
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that we search at night because people are home then, and a candle's light works well for searching in the dark.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: we search at the time when people are found in their homes, and a candle's light is good for searching.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the question from steps 8–10: why the search is at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The night is chosen for practical reasons, not because of a deadline. At night everyone is home, so no one forgets the search while busy outside. Also, a candle shows the cracks and holes well in the dark, but not in daylight.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the custom we keep today: searching for חמץ with a candle on the night of the fourteenth.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
At the time when people
are found in their homes,
and the light of the candle is good for searching.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁבְּנֵי אָדָם מְצוּיִין בְּבָתֵּיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of steps 8–10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning: a new reason for the timing
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The search should be timed by the deadline or by eagerness, which points to midday or morning.
steps.terutzMaskana: The night is chosen because people are home and candlelight searches well.

steps.title: A scholar should not start learning on the night of the search
steps.stepSummary: אביי concludes that a Torah scholar should not begin his regular learning session on the night of the fourteenth. He might get caught up and miss the בדיקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: therefore, a Torah scholar should not start his set learning time on the night after the thirteenth, the night of the fourteenth. His learning might pull him in, and he will end up missing the מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי draws a practical rule from the answer that the search is done at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the search must happen at night, that is exactly when a scholar usually sits down to learn. If he starts, his learning might pull him in and the time for the search will pass. So he should search first and not open his learning session.

keyTerms.meaning: The night leading into the fourteenth
His learning, his topic of study

steps.whatToRemember: We search for חמץ on the night of the fourteenth with a candle because people are home and candlelight searches well. So one should not begin learning then and risk missing the search.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the הלכה that one may not start learning or other activities close to the time of בדיקת חמץ.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Therefore,
a young Torah scholar
should not begin his set learning time
on the evening of the thirteenth
that leads into the fourteenth,
lest his learning draws him in,
and he comes to be held back from the מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical rule from the answer in step 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A Torah scholar should not begin his regular learning on the night of the fourteenth, so that he does not miss בדיקת חמץ.

steps.title: Who must check a house rented on the fourteenth
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק is asked whether the landlord or the renter must check a house rented out on the fourteenth.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב נחמן בר יצחק: If someone rents out a house on the fourteenth, who has to check it? Is it the landlord, because the חמץ is his? Or is it the renter, because the forbidden item is now in his space?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is asked. When a house changes hands on the fourteenth, who is responsible for the בדיקה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to look at it. The landlord owns the חמץ that was left in the house, so maybe he must check. The renter will live in the house over פסח, so the problem sits in his space, and maybe he must check.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked of him (a real question that needs an answer)
Landlord, the one who rents out the house
Renter, the one who rents the house

phrases.aramaic: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: They asked of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak:
One who rents out a house to his fellow on the fourteenth,
upon whom is it to search?
Is it upon the landlord to search,
since the chametz is his,
or perhaps it is upon the renter to search,
since the prohibited item stands in his domain?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new practical question about בדיקה after the discussion of the night-time timing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether ownership of the חמץ (landlord) or living in the space (renter) decides who must check.

steps.title: Proof from the renter's obligation of מזוזה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the renter must put up the מזוזה, which suggests that the renter also handles בדיקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone rents out a house to his fellow, the renter must put up a מזוזה for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question with a ruling about מזוזה. The renter is the one obligated there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that house-related מצוות fall on the person renting the house. If the renter handles the מזוזה, maybe he also handles the בדיקה.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who rents out a house to his fellow,
it is upon the renter to make a mezuzah for it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to settle the question in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That the renter must check for חמץ.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that puts the מזוזה obligation on the renter.

steps.title: מזוזה is different because it depends on the resident
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected because מזוזה is an obligation of whoever lives in the house. So the question about חמץ still needs an answer, which the next step gives.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, didn't רב משרשיא say that מזוזה is the obligation of the one who lives there? So here, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the מזוזה proof and asks the question again. The next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מזוזה is tied to whoever lives in the house, so naturally the renter does it. חמץ is different, because the landlord owns it, so the מזוזה case teaches nothing here.

keyTerms.meaning: An obligation on the one who lives there

phrases.english: There, didn't Rav Mesharshiya say:
Mezuzah is the obligation of the resident.
Here, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison between מזוזה and בדיקת חמץ entirely.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: מזוזה depends on who lives in the house, while the בדיקה question is about who owns the חמץ.

steps.title: It depends on when the keys were handed over
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק quotes a ברייתא. If the fourteenth began before the keys were handed over, the landlord checks. If it began after, the renter checks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said to them: We learned it. If someone rents out a house, and the fourteenth began before he gave the renter the keys, the landlord must check. If the fourteenth began after he gave him the keys, the renter must check.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the first question with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Handing over the keys is the moment the house becomes the renter's. Whoever controls the house when the time for checking arrives (the night of the fourteenth) is the one who must check.
steps.whatToRemember: The keys decide. Whoever holds the house when the fourteenth begins must check it.
steps.confusionAlert: Who owns the חמץ is not what decides. What decides is whether the keys were handed over before or after the fourteenth began.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said to them,
we have learned it:
One who rents out a house to his fellow,

phrases.aramaic: אִם עַד שֶׁלֹּא מָסַר לוֹ מַפְתְּחוֹת
phrases.english: if before he handed him the keys
the fourteenth began,
it is upon the landlord to search;
and if after he handed him the keys
the fourteenth began,
it is upon the renter to search.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק, תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question restated in step 15 ('הכא מאי').
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The handing over of the keys decides who must check.

steps.title: Is a rented house presumed already checked
steps.stepSummary: A second question asks whether a house rented on the fourteenth is presumed to have already been checked.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רב נחמן בר יצחק: If someone rents out a house on the fourteenth, do we assume it was already checked, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question starts. Can the renter assume the landlord already did the בדיקה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most people check on the night of the fourteenth. So the question is whether we can rely on that normal practice and treat the house as already checked.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: They asked of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak:
One who rents out a house to his fellow on the fourteenth,
is its presumption that it is checked,
or is its presumption not that it is checked?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעוֹ מִינֵּיהּ מֵרַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate question about the same rental case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a house rented on the fourteenth has a חזקה of being checked.

steps.title: Why not just ask the landlord
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges whether the question matters, since the renter could simply ask the landlord.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make? Let him just ask him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the question itself. It seems pointless, because the renter can just ask the landlord if he checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the landlord is available, there is no need for a presumption. The facts can simply be found out by asking.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: For what does it make a practical difference?
Let him ask him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the question in step 17 has any practical relevance.
steps.kashyaTarget: The relevance of the question in step 17.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is no need for a presumption when you can simply ask the landlord.

steps.title: The landlord is not around to ask
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the landlord is unavailable. The question is whether the renter must take the trouble to check.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where the landlord is not here to ask. Do we make the renter go to the trouble of checking, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the real case behind the question, and the question is restated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the landlord gone, the only way out is a presumption. If the house is presumed checked, the renter is spared the work. If not, he must check.

keyTerms.meaning: To burden, to make him go to the trouble

phrases.english: Where this one is not there to ask him.
As to burdening this one, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (the landlord is unavailable).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question seemed pointless because the landlord could be asked.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question applies when the landlord cannot be asked. It decides whether the renter must check.

steps.title: Everyone is believed about removing חמץ
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק begins his answer with a ברייתא: everyone, even women, slaves and minors, is believed about removing חמץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said to them: You learned it. Everyone is believed about removing חמץ, even women, even slaves, even minors.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק starts answering by quoting a ברייתא. The next step asks why these people are believed, and the argument is completed on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People who are usually not trusted as witnesses are believed here. This shows the rabbis were lenient about trust when it comes to בדיקה. That leniency will be used to support the presumption that a house is already checked.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said to them,
you have learned it:
Everyone is believed about the removal of chametz,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ נָשִׁים אֲפִילּוּ עֲבָדִים אֲפִילּוּ קְטַנִּים.
phrases.english: even women, even slaves, even minors.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק, תְּנֵיתוּהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the restated question in step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not finished yet. It begins with the ברייתא that everyone is believed about removing חמץ.

steps.title: Why are they believed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason these people are trusted, setting up the explanation that follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason they are believed?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא asks why women, slaves and minors are trusted, to prepare the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason they are trusted is what will connect the ברייתא to the rental question. The answer comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: What is the reason they are believed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ברייתא quoted in step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason women, slaves and minors are trusted about removing חמץ.
